say.text: Now the bedside. You reduce a groin lump, press a finger over the deep ring and ask him to cough.
This lump is an indirect hernia. Predict: does it come back while your finger holds the ring shut?

choices.label: It comes back medial to your finger
It stays away while the ring is held shut
It bulges out lateral to your finger
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which door the finger shuts. An indirect sac has to pass through the deep ring to reach the canal.
Tempting, because a direct sac does bulge medial to a finger. But this lump is indirect, so the finger is blocking its route.
An indirect sac enters through the deep ring, which the finger closes, so it cannot reappear medially while held.
The swelling stays away while the ring is held shut. Only a direct sac keeps bulging past the finger.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check the route, not the word: the finger stops an indirect sac, not a direct one.

say.text: Tempting, because a sac pushing out of a ring can look like it bulges lateral to whatever blocks it.
But the finger sits on the deep ring, the door an indirect sac uses, so the sac is held back rather than pushed past.
The swelling stays away while the ring is held shut.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so picture the finger pinching the neck: an indirect sac cannot get past it.

say.text: Right call. The finger closes the deep ring, the only door an indirect sac uses, so it stays away while held shut.
Two routes, two sites. An indirect sac comes through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, and runs down the canal.
A direct sac bulges through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the same vessels, through the posterior wall.
So the finger blocks one route, and a direct sac still bulges past it.
Same test on a new lump. You reduce it, hold the deep ring shut and ask him to cough.
This time the swelling still bulges medial to your finger. Which hernia is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether a sac that still bulges past the finger on the deep ring can have come through that ring.
Tempting, because indirect is the commoner hernia and you have just learned the finger test.
But an indirect sac travels through the deep ring, which your finger shuts, so it would not reappear medial to the finger.
A sac that still bulges medial to the finger comes through the posterior wall, so it is direct.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so let the finger decide: it blocks the indirect route, and a direct sac still shows.

say.text: Tempting, because a femoral hernia is also a groin lump, and a bulge near the tubercle can feel like one.
But a femoral hernia is placed by the pubic tubercle, below and lateral to it, and the finger test does not define it.
A swelling that stays medial to the finger over the deep ring is a direct inguinal hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the sites: inguinal types are judged against the vessels and the ring, femoral by the tubercle.

say.text: Right call. The sac still bulges medial to the finger, so it came through the posterior wall: direct.
At laparoscopy you look at the sac's neck against the inferior epigastric vessels.
Which description fits a direct sac?

choices.label: Lateral to the vessels, out through the deep ring
Medial to the vessels, through the posterior wall
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Go by the side of the vessels first, then by the route the sac takes through the wall.
Tempting, because direct sounds like it comes straight in from the front, so a lateral sac can feel direct.
But a lateral sac goes out through the deep ring and is indirect; a direct sac goes through the posterior wall, medial to the vessels.
So the side of the vessels and the wall the sac passes through decide the name, not how straight it looks.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so trust the route, not the word: lateral to the vessels is indirect, medial is direct.

say.text: Right call. A direct sac bulges through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, through the posterior wall.
In Zieman's three-finger test the index finger sits over the deep ring, the middle over the superficial ring and the ring finger over the saphenous opening.
An impulse felt under the middle finger suggests which hernia?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Each finger covers one ring. Find the ring under the middle finger, then ask which hernia comes through that ring.
Tempting, because the index finger sits on the deep ring, the door of the indirect sac, so it feels like the answer.
But the index finger is the indirect finger. The middle finger is the one that suggests a direct hernia.
So an impulse under the middle finger points to direct, and under the index finger to indirect.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pin each finger to its ring before you read the impulse.

say.text: Tempting, because the ring finger is the femoral finger, so the groin fingers can feel mixed up.
But an impulse on the ring finger suggests femoral. The middle finger is a different site, over the superficial ring.
So the middle finger's impulse suggests a direct hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so count the fingers from the deep ring outward: index, middle, ring.

say.text: Right call. The middle finger covers the superficial ring, and an impulse there suggests a direct hernia.
In the invagination test the little finger pushes the scrotal skin into the superficial ring.
The impulse is felt on the tip of the finger. Which hernia is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tip and pulp mark how deep the sac lies. Which sac travels along the canal from the deep ring?
Tempting, because the impulse sits in the scrotal skin, and direct is the sac most people picture at the superficial ring.
But the tip of the finger marks the indirect sac, which travels down the canal; the pulp marks the direct one.
So a tip impulse is indirect, and a pulp impulse is direct.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so match the finger part to depth: the tip is the deeper, indirect sac.

say.text: Tempting, because femoral is the other groin hernia, and you have just used the ring finger for it.
But the invagination test is the little finger at the superficial ring, not the femoral site under the ring finger.
A tip impulse on the little finger suggests indirect; a pulp impulse suggests direct.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the two tests apart: Zieman's ring finger is femoral, the invagination is tip against pulp.

say.text: Right call. A tip impulse on the little finger means an indirect hernia; a pulp impulse means direct.
A 68-year-old man has a lump near the pubic tubercle. Which description fits his hernia?

choices.label: Pear-shaped oblique swelling reaching the scrotum, reduces laterally
Globular swelling by the pubic tubercle that regularly reaches the scrotum
Globular swelling by the tubercle, reduces straight back, rarely scrotal
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Start with where the lump sits and how it reduces, then ask which sac follows the cord into the scrotum.
Tempting, because the scrotal swelling is the most visible sign, and the pear-shaped lump that reaches the scrotum is the picture people remember.
But that picture is the indirect hernia, which follows the cord down the canal and reduces upwards, laterally and backwards.
A direct hernia is a globular swelling by the pubic tubercle that rarely reaches the scrotum.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link the scrotum to the sac that follows the cord, not to the one that bulges through the posterior wall.

say.text: Tempting, because a globular lump by the tubercle looks like a direct hernia, so it seems to fit the scrotum too.
But a direct hernia rarely descends into the scrotum; it is the indirect hernia that commonly does.
So the direct hernia is globular by the tubercle, reduces straight backwards and stays out of the scrotum.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep shape and scrotum apart: the scrotum belongs to the indirect sac.

say.text: Right call. A direct hernia is a globular swelling by the pubic tubercle that reduces straight backwards and rarely reaches the scrotum.
A 3-month-old boy has a right inguinal hernia.
What is the underlying defect?

choices.label: Weak posterior wall of the canal
Defect in the transversalis fascia at Hesselbach's triangle
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether the sac is a passage the child was born with, or a weakness that develops in the wall.
Tempting, because a weak posterior wall is the cause you attach to the common groin hernia, and the canal is what you are picturing.
But that weakness is the acquired direct cause. A baby's indirect hernia is not a wall defect; it is a passage left open from birth.
The congenital cause is a patent processus vaginalis.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the causes by age: the child's is congenital, the adult direct one is acquired.

say.text: Tempting, because the transversalis fascia forms the floor of Hesselbach's triangle, where a direct hernia breaks through.
But in a child the defect is the processus vaginalis, a sac-shaped passage, not a fascial gap in the triangle.
The patent processus vaginalis is the congenital cause; the triangle defect belongs to the acquired direct hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask whether the defect is a passage the child was born with, or a weak wall.

say.text: Right call. An indirect hernia in a child is congenital, arising in a patent processus vaginalis that normally closes after the testis descends.
The processus vaginalis can stay open along its whole length, or only part of it.
Which pairing is right?

choices.label: Whole: funicular hernia; part: complete congenital hernia
Whole: direct hernia; part: indirect hernia
Whole: complete congenital hernia; part: funicular hernia
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Go by how far down the sac reaches: all the way to the testis, or stopping above it.
Tempting, because the funicular hernia sounds like the bigger one that reaches down the cord, so the two names are easy to swap.
But the rule is how far the process stays open: whole open reaches the testis, and that is the complete congenital hernia.
Only part open stops above the testis, and that is the funicular hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so count the extent: the whole process gives the complete hernia, part of it the funicular one.

say.text: Tempting, because both are groin lumps, so the direct and indirect names feel like the right labels for the two extents.
But the question is about the processus vaginalis, and a direct hernia is acquired, so it does not follow an open process.
Whole open is the complete congenital hernia; part open is the funicular hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep the extent of the sac apart from its route: direct and indirect describe the route.

say.text: Right call. A wholly open processus vaginalis gives a complete congenital hernia reaching the testis; a partly open one gives a funicular hernia stopping above it.
A 55-year-old woman has a lump that sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
Which hernia is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check the lump against the pubic tubercle first. Is it above and medial to it, where inguinal hernias emerge?
Tempting, because an indirect hernia is the commonest groin lump, so it is the reflex answer for any swelling by the groin.
But position decides here. An inguinal hernia emerges above and medial to the pubic tubercle; this lump sits below and lateral to it.
Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is the femoral hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so place the lump against the pubic tubercle before you name it.

say.text: Tempting, because a direct hernia sits near the pubic tubercle, so a groin lump by it can feel direct.
But a direct hernia emerges above and medial to the tubercle, through Hesselbach's triangle; this lump is below and lateral.
Below and lateral to the pubic tubercle is the femoral hernia.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so use the tubercle as the test for femoral: below and lateral means femoral.

say.text: Right call. A femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle; an inguinal hernia lies above and medial to it.
The anterior wall of the canal is the external oblique aponeurosis.
Which muscle reinforces that wall laterally?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about which muscle lies deep to the external oblique and reinforces the front of the canal.
Tempting, because the conjoint tendon is the strong band at the groin and lies beside the internal oblique, so it feels anterior.
But the conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall medially; the anterior wall is only reinforced laterally by the internal oblique.
So the anterior wall's lateral reinforcement is the internal oblique.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair each reinforcement with its wall: the conjoint tendon belongs to the posterior wall.

say.text: Right call. The anterior wall is reinforced laterally by the internal oblique; the conjoint tendon reinforces the posterior wall medially.
Three bedside tests, one rule: each follows the sac's route. The finger on the deep ring, the fingers in Zieman's test and the tip or pulp in the invagination test all do.
Indirect is congenital and can reach the scrotum; direct is acquired and stays near the tubercle. A femoral lump sits below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
